title: Ewedu with Kaun
author: Testimony Adewale
desc: The version that does use potash — a teaspoon boiled in the water before the leaves go in, then mashed with the ijabe and simmered one to two minutes.
longDesc: This is the counter-version to the blender-and-no-kaun ewedu, and it is the one the newspapers publish. A teaspoon of potash goes into boiling water first, the rinsed ewedu follows, and once the leaves soften they are mashed with the traditional mashing broom or blended if you have no ijabe. Then back to the pot with a stock cube and salt and a one-to-two-minute simmer. The alkali does two things — it preserves the green and it helps the leaf break down to the slippery consistency ewedu is wanted for — and the named food bloggers largely refuse it.
steps: Boil water with the potash for a few minutes.
Add the rinsed ewedu to the boiling potash water.
Once the leaves soften, mash them with the traditional mashing broom — or blend them if you have no ijabe.
Return to the pot, add the locust beans, the stock cube and salt.
chefTips: The potash goes into the water BEFORE the leaves, and boils for a few minutes first. That is the sequence and it differs from adding alkali at the end.
A teaspoon is the quantified figure. The same newspaper's other article says only 'a tiny amount', so a teaspoon is the number to work from.
If you are using baking soda rather than potash, add it near the END of cooking rather than the start — the two alkalis are not interchangeable in their timing.
One to two minutes at the end and no more. This is a much shorter cook than the no-kaun version, because the alkali has done the softening.
Kaun keeps the green vivid. That is its visible contribution and it is why the newspaper recipes use it.
For the version that refuses potash entirely and gets its viscosity from blending, see NGA002. Both are legitimate and the named bloggers are on the other side of this question.
Read NGA120 before using kaun. It is not chemically potash, and it carries a specific safety warning that matters in pregnancy.
commonMistakes: Adding the potash with the leaves rather than boiling it in the water first.
Using baking soda at the start, where potash goes.
More than a teaspoon, which tastes soapy.
Using kaun without reading the safety note.
sources: Adapted from the ewedu component of 'Amala and Abula: Treat yourself to amazing Yoruba staple', byline Testimony Ishola, Tribune Online. Quantities as printed: 2 cups of ewedu; 1 tablespoon of locust beans (iru); seasoning and salt to taste; 'Tiny amount of potash or baking soda'.

THE ONE-TEASPOON FIGURE comes from the second Tribune article, 'Abula: Mix of Gbegiri and ewedu with Amala', byline 'Our Reporter', which specifies 'Add a tea spoon of potash to boiling water'. That article otherwise gives no quantities at all. The teaspoon is used above because it is the only quantified potash figure for ewedu in any source consulted.

Method as printed: rinse; 'boil water with potash for a few minutes', then add the rinsed ewedu; once the leaves soften, 'mash with the traditional mashing broom (or blend if unavailable)'; return to pot with stock cube and salt; 'simmer 1–2 minutes'.

NOTE A PROCESSING-ORDER DIFFERENCE within the Tribune's own two articles: the second one blends the RAW washed leaves with a little warm water and adds the purée to boiling potash water — the reverse of every other source, which boils the leaves first and processes after. The order used above follows the quantified article.

THE FLAT CONTRADICTION ON POTASH, which is why this version is published separately from NGA002. Sisi Jemimah refuses it outright: 'Now, I don't cook with Kaun (Potash), but rest assured. blending does enhance the viscosity.' 9jafoodie's ewedu does not mention it and thickens with a tablespoon of blended egusi instead (NGA003). Tribune's Testimony Ishola calls for a 'tiny amount of potash or baking soda'; the second Tribune article quantifies it at a teaspoon. So the named bloggers avoid kaun for ewedu and get draw from blending or from egusi, while the newspaper recipes use it. Not reconciled — both are published.

A WITHIN-SITE SPLIT worth recording: 9jafoodie uses NO kaun in ewedu but half a teaspoon in okra (NGA015). That same okra page is the only source consulted that distinguishes the TIMING of the two alkalis — potash at the start, baking soda about two minutes before the end — which is the basis for the tip above.

ON WHAT THE ALKALI ACTUALLY DOES: 'Understanding Nigerian Condiments - Kaun (Akanwa)', on Funke Koleosho's blog with the post byline 'tasteofnigeria', lists ewedu under 'vegetable enhancement' but does NOT explain the mechanism. The explanation offered above — that it preserves the green and helps the leaf break down — is the standard account of what an alkali does to a leafy vegetable and is NOT asserted as sourced.
For what kaun is chemically and the safety warning that belongs with it, see NGA120.
reheating: Gentle heat with a splash of water. Do not boil.
healthBenefits: Jute leaf is high in vitamins A, C and E, calcium and iron.
Very low in calories and fat.
The mucilage is a soluble fibre.
Cooked briefly, which preserves more of the vitamin C.
culturalNote: That the newspapers use kaun and the named food bloggers largely refuse it is a real divide in Yoruba home cooking rather than a matter of accuracy. The alkali is the older practice and it does something a blender cannot quite replicate; the refusal is a modern, health-conscious position. Ibadan buka cooks mostly use it.
